components.note: 扌 (hand) — a hand doing the action
乚 (hook/bundle) — a bundle being fastened or pierced

example.hanzi: 我的手指被针扎了一下。
example.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒuzhǐ bèi zhēn zhā le yíxià.
example.english: My finger got pricked by a needle.
example.fact: 扎 has several readings: zhā is 'to prick' or 'to pitch' (扎营, to camp), zā is 'to tie up' (扎辫子, braid hair), and zhá appears in 挣扎 'to struggle'. Pick the reading by meaning.

components.note: 刂 (knife) — cutting a thing into shape, the sense of 'making'
巾 (jīn) is only a rough sound link to zhì

example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo wéijīn shì shǒugōng zhì de.
example.english: This scarf is handmade.
example.fact: Simplified 制 merges two older characters: 制 'to control, a system' (制度) and 製 'to make' (制造). So the same shape covers both meanings now, and context decides which one applies.

components.note: 方 (a flag, shown on the left) — a banner that rallied a clan
矢 (arrow) — warriors gathered under the banner

example.pinyin: Zhōngguó yǒu wǔshíliù gè mínzú.
example.english: China has fifty-six ethnic groups.
example.fact: 族 is the base of 民族 (nationality, ethnic group) and 家族 (family clan). As a modern suffix, it labels groups with shared habits: 上班族 (office workers), 月光族 (people who spend their whole salary each month).

components.note: 氵 (water) — bathing involves water
喿 (zào) gives the sound — a near match to zǎo

example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān wǎnshang dōu xǐzǎo.
example.english: I take a bath every evening.
example.fact: 澡 is almost never used alone: 洗澡 ('wash bath') is a verb-object phrase, so the verb can split around it — 洗了个澡 'took a bath', not 洗澡了个.

components.note: 火 (fire) — heat, hence burning
汤 (tāng) gives the sound — only the tone differs

example.pinyin: Xiǎoxīn, zhè bēi chá hěn tàng.
example.english: Careful, this cup of tea is scalding.
example.fact: 烫 is hotter than 热: it means 'hot enough to burn you', as in 烫手. The same character covers 烫头发 (to perm hair) and 烫衣服 (to iron clothes), both involving heat.

components.note: 亻 (person) — a person turning to the side
则 (zé) gives the sound — close to cè

example.pinyin: Qǐng cóng zuǒ cè tōngguò.
example.english: Please pass on the left side.
example.fact: 侧 means a side or flank, in compounds like 侧面 (profile, side view), 左侧 / 右侧 and 侧身 (to turn sideways). It is a little more formal than 边.

components.note: 食 (food) — a meal is about eating
The upper part is a rare composite (歺 + 又) that only loosely hints at the sound cān.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen yìqǐ qù chī wǎncān ba.
example.english: Let's go have dinner together.
example.fact: 餐 is the measure word of meals: 一日三餐 (three meals a day). It sounds more formal than 饭, as in 早餐 (breakfast), 西餐 (Western food) and 用餐 ('to dine'), and 餐厅 is a restaurant or dining hall.

components.note: A leg: the round upper part is the knee or kneecap and the lower part is the foot; this led to 'foot' and then 'enough'.

example.pinyin: Qián yǐjīng zúgòu le.
example.english: The money is already enough.
example.fact: 足 is the written word for 'foot' (spoken Chinese says 脚), and it is the root of 足球 (football). It also means 'enough', as in 足够 and 充足, and is the radical in many foot-related characters.

components.note: Its modern shape (日 above 勿) is a worn-down form, so the parts are not a dependable clue; learn it as a whole.

example.pinyin: Zhège wèntí bù róngyì huídá.
example.english: This question is not easy to answer.
example.fact: 易 has two main senses: 'easy' (容易) and 'to change or exchange' (交易 trade, 易经 the Book of Changes). In 容易 the second syllable is neutral in tone.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — nails are made of metal
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — it matches 钉 exactly

example.pinyin: Qiáng shàng dìng zhe yì kē dīngzi.
example.english: There is a nail hammered into the wall.
example.fact: 钉 is a noun 'nail' read dīng, and a verb 'to nail' read dìng, as in 钉钉子. So the sentence 钉钉子 contains both: dìng dīngzi.

components.note: Often explained as a stand for offerings or an ancestral altar; the grammatical meaning 'moreover' is a later borrowed use.

example.pinyin: Zhège fángjiān dà érqiě gānjìng.
example.english: This room is big and also clean.
example.fact: Alone 且 is literary, but it is common in 而且 ('moreover', as in 不但……而且……), 并且 and 况且. It can mean 'for the time being' in expressions like 暂且 and 姑且.

components.note: 巳 forms the upper part of the simplified shape
廾 (two hands) — hands holding something, from the older character 異

example.pinyin: Liǎng guó de wénhuà chāyì hěn dà.
example.english: The cultures of the two countries differ greatly.
example.fact: 异 is the simplified form of 異 and means 'different' or 'strange'. It builds 差异 (difference), 异常 (abnormal), 惊异 and 异国 (a foreign land); it is mostly written, not spoken.

components.note: 氵 (water) — liquid dripping through a hole
屚 (lòu) — dripping rain, and also gives the sound

example.pinyin: Wūdǐng lòu shuǐ le.
example.english: The roof is leaking.
example.fact: 漏 means both 'to leak' (漏水, 漏气) and, figuratively, 'to omit, to miss': 漏了一个字 is 'missed a word'. 泄漏 and 漏洞 (loophole, security hole) are common in news and tech.

components.note: 青 (qīng) — clear and calm like green nature
争 (zhēng) gives only a loose sound hint

example.pinyin: Túshūguǎn lǐ hěn jìng.
example.english: It is very quiet in the library.
example.fact: 静 is quieter than 安静 only in tone: 请安静 is the normal polite 'be quiet', while 静 mostly forms compounds: 平静 (calm), 冷静 (composed), 寂静 (silent) and 静止 (still).

components.note: 口 (mouth) — a sound uttered by the mouth
喜 (xǐ) — joy, also hints at the sound

example.pinyin: Háizi xīxī de xiào le.
example.english: The child laughed with a giggle.
example.fact: 嘻 is an onomatopoeic syllable for giggling; doubled as 嘻嘻 (heehee) or in 笑嘻嘻 'beaming'. It is also the first half of 嘻哈, the transliteration of 'hip-hop'.

excludeSuggestion: Mostly onomatopoeic; appears in 嘻嘻 and 嘻哈 rather than as a standalone word.

components.note: 女 (woman) — marks the female form
尔 (ěr) — an old word for 'you', which also gives the sound

example.pinyin: Nǐ jīntiān kàn qǐlái hěn kāixīn.
example.english: You look very happy today.
example.fact: 妳 is a feminine 'you' that writers coined in the early twentieth century; it is still seen in Taiwan and Hong Kong, but in the mainland and in speech everyone uses 你, which is gender-neutral.

excludeSuggestion: Variant form of 你; the female 'you' occurs mainly in Taiwanese/Hong Kong writing.

components.note: 龶 (a plant-like form) — a plant fibre being spun
糸 (silk thread) — raw, undyed silk

example.pinyin: Wǒ chī sù, bù chī ròu.
example.english: I'm a vegetarian; I don't eat meat.
example.fact: 素 originally meant undyed raw silk, hence 'plain, unadorned'. It forms 吃素 (to eat vegetarian), 素菜, 素质 (quality) and 元素 (element), and is the opposite of 荤 (meat-based).

components.note: 欠 (a yawning mouth) — an open-mouthed craving
谷 (gǔ) gives a rough sound clue for yù

example.pinyin: Háizi de qiúzhīyù hěn qiáng.
example.english: The child has a strong desire for knowledge.
example.fact: 欲 names a 'desire' noun and attaches to words such as 食欲 (appetite), 求知欲 (thirst for knowledge) and 购买欲 (urge to buy). As a verb, 欲 + verb is a formal 'about to', as in 欲言又止 'wanting to speak but holding back'.

components.note: An early picture of the outer ear; the modern form is simplified but the idea is still an ear.

example.pinyin: Tā zài wǒ ěr biān xiǎoshēng shuōhuà.
example.english: He spoke quietly by my ear.
example.fact: In daily speech the ear is 耳朵; the single character 耳 is used in compounds like 耳机 (earphones) and 耳环 (earring). In classical writing 耳 also marks 'and that's all', like 而已.

components.note: The pieces of 率 (a cap, string-like strokes, 十) do not form a clear picture; learn it as a unit.

example.hanzi: 这家工厂的成功率很高。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngchǎng de chénggōnglǜ hěn gāo.
example.english: This factory has a high success rate.
example.fact: 率 has two readings: lǜ means 'rate' (效率 efficiency, 汇率 exchange rate, 概率 probability) and shuài means 'to lead' or 'frank' (率领, 坦率). Statistics words almost always end in -率 lǜ.

components.note: 矢 (arrow) — arrows were used for measuring length
委 (wěi) gives a rough sound clue

example.pinyin: Tā bǐ gēge ǎi yìdiǎn.
example.english: He is a bit shorter than his brother.
example.fact: 矮 is the opposite of 高 for height of people, buildings and furniture; 低 is used for levels such as 低温. Telling someone 你很矮 is quite blunt, so use 不太高 for politeness.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — a loud sound from the mouth
孔 (kǒng) gives a rough sound clue

example.pinyin: Bié duì wǒ hǒu, wǒ tīng de jiàn.
example.english: Don't yell at me; I can hear you.
example.fact: 吼 is stronger than 喊: it is an angry or powerful shout, and also the roar of a lion or the howl of wind. 怒吼 means 'to roar in anger', and 狮子吼 is a lion's roar.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — arranging by words and orders
殳 (shū) gives a loose sound clue to shè

example.pinyin: Gōngsī de zǒngbù shè zài Shànghǎi.
example.english: The company's headquarters is based in Shanghai.
example.fact: 设 is the root of 设计 (design), 设备 (equipment), 设置 (to set) and 假设 (to suppose). Alone, as in 设在 'is located at', it is a formal verb used for institutions and offices.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — giving by hand
肙 (yuān) gives the sound — close to juān

example.pinyin: Tā xiàng zāiqū juān le yìxiē qián.
example.english: He donated some money to the disaster area.
example.fact: 捐 is the usual verb for donations: 捐款 (donate money), 捐血 (give blood) and 捐赠 (to give, more formal). As a noun it can mean 'a levy or tax', as in older 税捐 or 苛捐杂税 ('exorbitant taxes').

components.note: 米 (rice) — refined grain, the original sense of 'pure'
青 (qīng) gives the sound — close to jīng

example.pinyin: Tā de jīngshén zhuàngtài hěn hǎo.
example.english: His mental state is very good.
example.fact: 精 began as 'polished rice' and grew to mean 'refined, essence, skilful': 精彩 (wonderful), 精神 (spirit), 精通 (be proficient in), 精确 (precise). 精 can also mean a spirit, as in 妖精.

components.note: 阝 (mound/wall) — a barrier between places
鬲 (gé) gives the sound — it matches 隔 exactly

example.pinyin: Wǒ zhù zài nǐ jiā gébì.
example.english: I live next door to you.
example.fact: 隔 describes an interval or barrier: 隔壁 (next door), 隔夜 (overnight) and 隔音 (soundproof). With time words it means 'every other': 隔一天 is every second day, and 隔了很久 is 'after a long gap'.

components.note: Older explanations see a hand measuring a span, but the modern shape is too reduced to show the picture clearly.

example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ chǐzi jiè gěi wǒ.
example.english: Please lend me the ruler.
example.fact: In the traditional measure, 1 尺 (市尺) is one third of a metre, so 三尺 is about a metre. It forms 尺子 (a ruler), 尺寸 (size, dimensions) and 卷尺 (tape measure); in music, 尺 is also a note name.

components.note: 木 (wood) — tables are made of wood
卓 (zhuō) gives the sound — it matches 桌 exactly

example.pinyin: Shū fàng zài zhuōzi shàng.
example.english: The book is on the table.
example.fact: 桌 appears mostly in 桌子 (table) and 书桌 (desk). It is also the measure word for dinner tables: 一桌菜 means 'a table full of dishes', and 开了十桌 'ten tables were set up for the banquet'.

components.note: 木 (tree) — the measure word is for plants
果 (guǒ) gives the sound — rhymes closely with kē

example.pinyin: Yuànzi lǐ yǒu yì kē dà shù.
example.english: There is a big tree in the yard.
example.fact: 棵 is the measure word for whole plants and trees — 一棵树, 一棵白菜 (a head of cabbage), 一棵草. Flowers use 朵, and leaves use 片, so don't use 棵 for those.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — talk or sounds
罗 (luó) gives the sound — only the tone differs

example.pinyin: Tā shuōhuà hěn luōsuo.
example.english: He is long-winded when he speaks.
example.fact: 啰 occurs in 啰嗦 (also 啰唆), 'long-winded, nagging'. It can be repeated as 啰里啰嗦 for emphasis, and 嗦 is neutral toned in speech: luōsuo.

excludeSuggestion: Bound character: it essentially occurs only in 啰嗦 and similar words.

components.note: ⺈ (a claw/hand shape) — one hand pulling an object
彐 (hand) — the second hand pulling the other way

example.pinyin: Liǎng gè háizi zài zhēng wánjù.
example.english: The two children are fighting over a toy.
example.fact: 争 means to contend for something, so it fits 争取 (strive for), 争论 (debate) and 争吵 (quarrel). 争 is the simplified form of 爭, which shows two hands pulling a thing in opposite directions.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — the old sense 'beard' on the chin
古 (gǔ) gives a loose sound hint to hú

example.pinyin: Nǐ bié húshuō, zhè bú shì zhēn de.
example.english: Don't talk nonsense; it isn't true.
example.fact: 胡 once labelled non-Han peoples to the north and west, which is why imported things carry it: 胡椒 (pepper), 胡萝卜 (carrot), 胡桃 (walnut). On its own it means 'recklessly': 胡说 (talk nonsense), 胡闹 (act up).

components.note: 欠 (a yawning mouth, 'owe/lack') — money owed or lacking, hinting at funds

example.pinyin: Zhè kuǎn shǒujī hěn shòu huānyíng.
example.english: This model of phone is very popular.
example.fact: 款 has two daily uses: money (付款 pay, 存款 deposit, 贷款 loan) and 'style/model' as a measure word: 一款手机 'a phone model', 新款 'new style'. It also counts clauses in a contract or law.

components.note: 囗 (enclosure) — something enclosed on all sides
韦 (wéi) gives the sound — it matches 围 exactly

example.pinyin: Dàjiā wéi zhe zhuōzi zuòxià.
example.english: Everyone sat around the table.
example.fact: 围 is the verb 'to surround', with 围着 (around) for position. It also gives 周围 (surroundings), 围巾 (scarf) and 围棋, the board game Go, named for the idea of surrounding territory.

components.note: 田 (field) — the stomach pictured as a pouch filled with grain
⺼ (flesh) — a body organ

example.pinyin: Wǒ de wèi yǒudiǎn téng.
example.english: My stomach hurts a little.
example.fact: 胃 is the organ itself, whereas the belly is 肚子, so Chinese has two words where English has one 'stomach'. 胃口 ('stomach mouth') means 'appetite', and also 'taste' or 'liking' in a figurative sense.

components.note: 兄 (older brother) — a group of kin and allies
尚 (shàng) gives a loose sound hint to dǎng

example.hanzi: 他加入了一个新的政党。
example.pinyin: Tā jiārù le yí gè xīn de zhèngdǎng.
example.english: He joined a new political party.
example.fact: 党 is the word for a political party (政党, 党员 party member), and most often hints at the Communist Party in mainland context. Casually, -党 is a suffix for fans or camps, such as 甜党 / 咸党 in the sweet-or-salty tofu pudding debate.

components.note: 木 (tree) — the original sense is a kind of pear tree
土 (tǔ) gives the sound — a close match

example.pinyin: Wǒmen yào dùjué làngfèi.
example.english: We must put an end to waste.
example.fact: 杜 as a verb sits mostly in 杜绝 ('to eliminate'); it is also a surname, famous for the poet 杜甫. The original sense, a pear-like tree, is rare now.

components.note: A picture of an old garment, showing the collar at the top and the two sleeves on the sides.

example.pinyin: Tā chuānzhe yí jiàn báiyī.
example.english: He is wearing a white garment.
example.fact: 衣 is the base of 衣服 (clothes) and 上衣 (top), and as a left-hand radical appears as 衤. The measure word for clothes is 件.

components.note: 刂 (knife) — carving with a blade
亥 (hài) gives a rough sound clue to kè

example.pinyin: Xiànzài shì sān diǎn yí kè.
example.english: It's now a quarter past three.
example.fact: 刻 means 'quarter hour' (一刻 = 15 min), so 三点一刻 is 3:15 and 差一刻 'a quarter to'. The idea of carving also yields 立刻 and 此刻 'at this moment'.

components.note: Often explained as breath (丂) escaping and spreading (八), a good fit for a sighing particle.

example.pinyin: Dàfēng qǐ xī yún fēiyáng.
example.english: A great wind rises, the clouds fly high.
example.fact: 兮 is a classical particle, comparable to 'oh!', used for rhythm in verse like the 楚辞 (Songs of Chu). The example line is attributed to the Han founder Liu Bang; you will not hear 兮 in modern speech.

excludeSuggestion: Classical-only particle; not used in modern Mandarin.

components.note: A picture of a dog seen from the side, with the dot as the tail; it also gives the radical 犭.

example.hanzi: 警犬找到了失踪的孩子。
example.pinyin: Jǐngquǎn zhǎodào le shīzōng de háizi.
example.english: The police dog found the missing child.
example.fact: 犬 is the literary or technical word for dog, while 狗 is the spoken one. It appears in 警犬, 导盲犬 (guide dog), 宠物犬 and 犬齿 (canine tooth).

components.note: 木 (wood) — furniture made of wood
巨 (jù) gives the sound — a loose match to guì

example.pinyin: Yīfu dōu zài yīguì lǐ.
example.english: The clothes are all in the wardrobe.
example.fact: 柜 in 柜子 means a cupboard or cabinet, and in 衣柜 (wardrobe) or 书柜 (bookcase). 柜台 is a shop 'counter', so 去柜台付款 means 'pay at the counter'.

components.note: 良 (liáng) — good; it also gives the sound
阝 (a city or place) — a man from a good place

example.hanzi: 新郎穿着一身黑色的西装。
example.pinyin: Xīnláng chuānzhe yì shēn hēisè de xīzhuāng.
example.english: The groom is wearing a black suit.
example.fact: 郎 once was an official title and came to mean 'young man'. It survives in 新郎 (groom), 郎才女貌 ('talented man, beautiful woman') and in 牛郎 of the legend 牛郎织女, the Cowherd and Weaver Girl.

excludeSuggestion: Bound character: mainly occurs in compounds like 新郎 or 牛郎, rarely alone.

components.note: 艹 (grass) — the plant meaning
沙 (shā) gives the sound — it matches 莎 exactly

example.hanzi: 莎士比亚是英国最有名的作家。
example.pinyin: Shāshìbǐyà shì Yīngguó zuì yǒumíng de zuòjiā.
example.english: Shakespeare is Britain's most famous writer.
example.fact: 莎 is a transliteration character used in foreign names, as in 莎士比亚 (Shakespeare) and 莎拉 (Sarah). Its original meaning is a sedge plant, which is read suō in 莎草.

excludeSuggestion: Occurs almost only in transliterated foreign names (e.g. 莎士比亚).

components.note: 十 (ten) — completeness, 'all kinds of things'
尃 (fū) gives a loose sound hint

example.pinyin: Zhè zuò bówùguǎn hěn dà.
example.english: This museum is very large.
example.fact: 博 means 'wide, abundant' and builds 博物馆 (museum, 'wide-things hall'), 博士 (doctorate holder) and 渊博 (erudite). 博客 is the borrowed word for 'blog', and 赌博 is gambling.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — a hand jabbing something
甬 (yǒng) gives the sound — a rough match

example.pinyin: Tā yòng gùnzi tǒng le tǒng niǎowō.
example.english: He poked the bird's nest with a stick.
example.fact: 捅 literally 'to poke', and a colourful figurative use is 捅马蜂窝 ('poke the hornets' nest'), meaning to stir up trouble. 捅娄子 means to cause a mess, and 捅破 'to puncture or reveal'.

meanings: to carry level with both hands

components.note: 立 (stand) — standing straight, upright
耑 (duān) gives the sound — it matches 端 exactly

example.pinyin: Fúwùyuán duān lái le yì wǎn tāng.
example.english: The waiter brought over a bowl of soup.
example.fact: 端 as a verb is carrying a bowl or tray level with both hands, unlike 拿 (hold) or 提 (carry hanging). It is also the root of 端午 (Dragon Boat Festival) and 极端 (extreme), where it means 'end'.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — the hand closing on something
屋 (wū) gives the sound — close in the final vowel

example.pinyin: Tā jǐnjǐn wò zhù le wǒ de shǒu.
example.english: He held my hand tightly.
example.fact: 握 is the verb in 握手 (shake hands) and 握拳 (clench a fist). 把握 is both 'to grasp' and 'confidence': 有把握 means 'to be sure of success'.

components.note: A picture of a cowrie shell with its slit, which was used as money in ancient China.

example.hanzi: 海边有很多漂亮的贝壳。
example.pinyin: Hǎibiān yǒu hěn duō piàoliang de bèiké.
example.english: There are many beautiful shells at the seaside.
example.fact: Because shells were once money, 贝 is the radical for wealth: 财, 货, 买, 贵, 贫. 贝壳 means 'shell', and 宝贝 ('precious shell') is a term of endearment for a baby or darling.

components.note: 氵 (water) — liquid
十 (shí) — a loose sound link to zhī

example.pinyin: Wǒ zǎoshang xǐhuan hē chéngzhī.
example.english: I like to drink orange juice in the morning.
example.fact: 汁 is the liquid pressed or cooked from food, as in 果汁 (fruit juice) and 肉汁 (gravy). Compared with 汤, which is broth, 汁 is a thicker or concentrated liquid.
